angle: The nine-mana commander is a turn-nine event — 10,000 goldfish games say so — but his Eminence discount is a turn-zero engine, so this deck wins from the command zone without ever paying for him, and its single most explosive verified weapon lives in the sideboard behind a bracket dial.

teases: THE 8.989 PROBLEM: ten thousand goldfish games say your commander is a turn-nine event — and the deck wins anyway
MIIRYM MATH: one five-mana cast, two free queens, 64 damage — checker-stamped
THE SIDEBOARD KILL: our first verified line that isn't in the 99, and the bracket dial it turns from 3 to 4
38 DRAGONS ON THE BENCH: every one judged, three swaps ordered

departments.note: The Ur-Dragon at hero scale from the pilot's printing — art by Jaime Jones (this issue's Featured Artist; the credit line under the art sets up the department). Tagline 'Nine mana. Worth it.' from issue.json, verbatim. The dominant coverline names verified stack 001's maximum: 15 Dragon Tempest triggers at X=17. Both violators are true: three checker-passed case files, and a commander cast by turn 6 in exactly zero of 10,000 goldfish runs — the honesty IS the hook.

Two-bucket contents (THIS ISSUE'S DECK / EVERY ISSUE) plus the tier legend printed in full — Vol. 005 may be somebody's first. The one-line promise for The Kill should read 'two kills you own, and one you have to ask the table for' — the sideboard-conditional A-003 is flagged from the very first page, never sprung on the reader.

departments.headline: NINE MANA, NEVER PAID
departments.dek: What kind of deck builds around a commander it casts in 13.5% of games? One that figured out the commander was never the point: his discount works from the command zone starting turn zero, and the payoff layer does the killing.

callouts.title: RIG THE DISCOUNT
callouts.text: Turns one through three you are a mana deck: rocks, Farseek, Nature's Lore — and above all the cost reducers, because they, not land drops, compress a nine-drop curve into a castable one. The goldfish is blunt: some ramp or fixing arrives by turn 6 in 75.6% of games, but a reducer in only 42.9%. Treat Urza's Incubator like an engine piece, because it is one.

callouts.title: DEPLOY INTO THE PAYOFFS
callouts.text: Turns four through six, land the cheap payoff layer first — Dragon Tempest at two, Temur Ascendancy at three — then feed it Dragons in waves, not all at once. Past critical mass every new Dragon draws cards, deals damage, and (with Miirym down) copies itself. Across four players, one wrath is near-certain; deploy accordingly.

callouts.title: PICK YOUR WINDOW
callouts.text: Turn seven onward is the capstone phase. The pivot is concrete: a haste enabler on the table plus two or three Dragons deployable in one turn — or Tiamat or the commander resolving. That turn you flip from control seat to beatdown, and every passive turn after it is a free draw step for three opponents.

captions.The Ur-Dragon: **THE DISCOUNT, NOT THE DRAGON:** Eminence takes {1} off every other Dragon spell from the command zone, all game, without him ever being cast — the engine you are guaranteed on turn zero.
captions.Urza's Incubator: **THE REAL RAMP:** Dragon spells cost {2} less, stacking with Eminence for {3} total. The goldfish model calls cost reducers the deck's real curve fixer — this is the best of them.
captions.Dragon Tempest: **LAND IT BEFORE THE WAVE:** haste for every flier entering, plus damage per Dragon entering equal to your Dragon count. It converts deployment into removal — and it stars in two of this issue's three case files.

pilot_tips.text: Lead with Dragonspeaker Shaman early and be glad when it eats a removal spell — every answer spent on a two-mana discount is one that never reaches your payoff layer.

departments.pull_quote: The Ur-Dragon is not the plan. His discount is.

departments.headline: EMINENCE DOMAIN
departments.dek: What is the command zone guarantee worth when the guaranteed card costs nine mana? Everything — because this commander's best ability works from the zone, which makes him the one commander in the format you should almost never cast.
departments.body: Start with the guarantee (CR 903.4): your commander is the only card you always have — and The Ur-Dragon inverts what that usually means, because Eminence is a static discount that applies while he sits in the command zone. You are not guaranteed a body; you are guaranteed a rules engine. The tax math (CR 903.8) makes the inversion policy: first cast nine (seven with Urza's Incubator out), second cast eleven, third cast thirteen — at those prices recasting is not a plan, it is a catastrophe, so protection beats speed by a mile (strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance), and the frame's advice stands: hold Teferi's Protection-class cover for the one turn he actually comes down. Better still, don't cast him at all: Hellkite Courser's trigger loans him from the command zone for one attack — draw per attacking Dragon, free permanent from hand — and 903.8's tax counts casts from the command zone, which a Courser loan never is; even if he dies mid-loan, 903.9a returns him home untaxed. Color identity: five colors lock nothing out — the cost is paid entirely by the manabase, and deck-facts prices it exactly (black needs 36 sources by Karsten math and the lands supply 11; white 22 against 9). The 21-damage clock is real but it is a coincidence, and here is the arithmetic the table gets wrong: unassisted he needs three connections (10+10 is one point short), and even Atarka's double strike stops at 20 — one short again. Only Thrakkus doubling his power first turns one swing lethal. The political read: this commander is face-up information from turn zero, so the table prices in the ending before you play a land. That is the tax Eminence never discounts — and the Politics Table department is about paying it on your schedule, not theirs.

captions.Hellkite Courser: **THE LOAN OFFICER:** puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone, hasty, for one attack — the trigger without the nine mana, the tax never accrues, and he goes home at end step.
captions.Teferi's Protection: **THE INSURANCE POLICY:** a taxed recast at eleven mana is a price this deck cannot pay — so the turn he finally lands is the turn this card was saved for.

pilot_tips.text: Rent before you buy: a Courser loan gets the attack trigger for five mana and dodges the commander tax entirely — the tax counts casts from the command zone, and a loan is not a cast.

departments.pull_quote: You are not guaranteed a body. You are guaranteed a discount — and it never dies, never taxes, and never taps out.

departments.headline: THE 8.989 PROBLEM
departments.dek: How slow is a nine-mana commander, exactly? We ran the list 10,000 times on seed 42 and got a number with three decimal places — and a deck that turns out to be built, in every measurable way, to not care.

callouts.title: THE HEADLINE NUMBER
callouts.text: Commander mean cast turn 8.989, median 9. Cast by turn 6: 0.0% — zero runs in ten thousand. Cast at all by turn 10: 13.5% (1,352 runs). The histogram: 183 casts on turn 7, 96 on turn 8, 626 on turn 9, 447 on turn 10, and 8,648 games where he never left home.

callouts.title: THE HANDS ARE FINE
callouts.text: Keep rate on the first seven: 76%. Mean mulligans: 0.298. The deck's opening hands are not the problem — the top of its curve is, and the hands are judged on whether they bridge to it.

callouts.title: THE LANDS QUIT EARLY
callouts.text: Land drop hit rate: 88.2% on turn 3, 50.1% by turn 6, 35.5% by turn 10. Mean available mana at turn 6 is 4.947. After turn 4, this deck's mana growth comes from rocks and Treasures, not land drops — plan your big turn around that.

callouts.title: THE REAL CURVE FIXER
callouts.text: Ramp or fixing drawn by turn 6: 75.6%. A cost reducer by turn 6: only 42.9%. The 'turn-5 Ur-Dragon hand' — reducer plus ramp together — assembles by turn 6 in just 29.4% of games. The reducers are the scarce resource; the mulligan department drills exactly this.

callouts.title: THE COVER YOU HOLD
callouts.text: A protection spell is in hand by turn 6 in 66.4% of games. That is the number that authorizes the whole commit-through-cover playbook — two games in three, the wave can be insured.

captions.Herald's Horn: **MEASURED, NOT MODELED:** the simulator does not model cost reducers — so every commander-lateness figure on this page is the conservative ceiling, and cards like this are why real games run faster.

pilot_tips.text: Weight artifact mana above land count when sequencing: the sim shows land drops decaying to 50.1% by turn 6, so the rock you cast on turn two is still paying on turn nine.

departments.pull_quote: Zero commander casts by turn six in ten thousand games — and the deck is fine with that.
departments.note: The stated-assumptions box is non-negotiable and matters doubly here: the model simulates resource development, not games, and it does not model cost reducers, rituals, or extra draw — so the commander figures are honestly pessimistic, which is exactly the direction of error this issue's thesis can afford. Cite every figure exactly as printed above; no rounding 8.989 to 9.

departments.headline: ROLL FOR DAMAGE
departments.dek: One combat connection, one d20, fifteen tokens — and suddenly there are fifteen triggers on the stack reading seventeen Dragons each. The checker walked all 255 points of it, and then did the same for the Miirym cascade.

callouts.title: THE CONNECTION
callouts.text: Case A-001's scene: Dragon Tempest, Ancient Gold Dragon, and Miirym on your battlefield; Ancient Gold Dragon has just dealt combat damage to a 30-life opponent, and the d20 comes up 15. Fifteen 1/1 Faerie Dragons enter — simultaneously, as one event.

callouts.title: ONE EVENT, FIFTEEN TRIGGERS
callouts.text: Dragon Tempest triggers once per Dragon entering, and one event with fifteen occurrences means fifteen separate damage triggers (plus fifteen haste triggers). Each one picks its own target as it goes on the stack — creature, player, planeswalker, or battle.

callouts.title: MIIRYM SITS THIS OUT
callouts.text: The instinct says Miirym doubles the tokens. The rules say no: her trigger reads 'nontoken', and every Faerie Dragon is a token. Zero copies — the checker confirmed it, and knowing what your board does NOT do is worth as much as knowing what it does.

callouts.title: SEVENTEEN, FIFTEEN TIMES
callouts.text: X is read when each trigger resolves: seventeen Dragons — two originals plus fifteen tokens (Tempest itself is an enchantment and doesn't count). No ramp-up, no decay: 255 damage on offer, with a real priority window between every resolution. The 30-life opponent dies to the second trigger pointed their way.

callouts.title: THE CASCADE
callouts.text: Case A-002 asks the other engine question: Lathliss resolving under Miirym, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks, and Dragon Tempest. Panharmonicon doubles every trigger in the chain — Miirym fires twice, two nonlegendary queens enter, and the full tally from one five-mana cast is 64 damage across twelve independently targeted instances. The verified board kills a 32-life opponent outright.

callouts.title: WHY IT STOPS
callouts.text: The copies never copy themselves: every 'nontoken' clause in the chain excludes the tokens' own entries, which is precisely what keeps the cascade finite and the deck at bracket 3. The engine is explosive because it ends — and the checker signed the ending.

captions.Ancient Gold Dragon: **THE DIE ROLLER:** combat damage to a player rolls a d20 and makes that many 1/1 Faerie Dragons — each one a fresh Dragon entering for the whole payoff layer. A mid-table roll is routinely lethal.
captions.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: **THE DOUBLER WITH A RULE:** every nontoken Dragon arrives twice — but read the word 'nontoken'. In A-001 she copies nothing at all; in A-002 she is the whole show.
captions.Lathliss, Dragon Queen: **ONE CAST, THREE QUEENS:** under Miirym and Panharmonicon, one Lathliss becomes three — and 64 damage rides along across twelve triggers.
captions.Panharmonicon: **THE TRIGGER TAX REFUND:** it doubles any trigger a creature's entry causes — it does not care whether the ability says 'Dragon', 'creature', or 'nontoken Dragon'. Twelve resolutions from one spell.
captions.Terror of the Peaks: **36 OF THE 64:** each entering creature deals its power to any target — in the verified cascade, six 6-damage instances, more than half the total.

pilot_tips.text: Stack the trigger you need most LAST — triggers resolve last-in-first-out, so if a blocker must die before your lethal triggers land, place its trigger on top.
Count your response windows before you celebrate: priority passes between every Tempest and Valkas resolution, so a single removal spell mid-chain lowers X for every trigger still waiting.

departments.pull_quote: Fifteen triggers, seventeen damage each, and a response window between every one.
departments.note: The marquee spread of the volume: A-001 as the numbered sequence, A-002 as the second feature. Dossier pointers on both: 'FULL DOSSIER: JUDGE'S DESK A-001 →' and 'A-002 →'. Then a clearly-labeled sidebar in a scenario-box — 'THE KILL YOU HAVE TO ASK FOR' — states plainly that a third verified line exists (Savage Ventmaw + Aggravated Assault, unbounded extra combats, +1 mana per cycle) but Aggravated Assault is in the SIDEBOARD, not the 99: the line is live only after the bracket-4 swap, floor 3→4. Point to Upgrade Watch for the swap and Judge's Desk A-003 for the proof. Do not style the sidebar as a lesser fact — it is the first verified line in any issue that lives in a sideboard, and the novelty is the story.

departments.headline: DRAGONS CAN'T BLUFF
departments.dek: The table sees a five-colour Ur-Dragon deck and prices in the ending before you play your second land — so how do you survive being the scariest deck at the table during the exact turns you are the weakest?

callouts.title: LOOK LIKE MANA
callouts.text: For turns one through four you are the control/value seat, and your job is to look like lands: rocks, Farseek, Dragon's Hoard, and Urza's Incubator draw almost no interaction on their own. The goldfish says you have 4.947 mana and 1.536 bodies at turn 6 — your actual threat is years behind your perceived one, so let the perception idle.

callouts.title: THE TELLS ARE ENCHANTMENTS
callouts.text: What flips the table's read is not a Dragon — it's the payoff layer. Experienced tables know what Dragon Tempest and Temur Ascendancy mean here, so deploy the cheap payoff the same turn you deploy Dragons into it, never a turn early as an invitation.

callouts.title: THE COUNTDOWN CARDS
callouts.text: The signals that flip you to archenemy hardest, in order: Tiamat resolving (five cards to hand is a public countdown), Hellkite Courser (everyone knows what it fetches), and any haste enabler with five-plus mana open. Sequence the scariest piece last — after the table's removal is spent.

callouts.title: COMMIT THROUGH COVER
callouts.text: When the pivot window opens — haste enabler plus two or three deployable Dragons — commit through held protection and count all three opponents' open mana first. You hold protection by turn 6 in 66.4% of games; you rarely get a second window. And never cast protection proactively: it telegraphs the big turn a full rotation early.

captions.Tiamat: **THE PUBLIC COUNTDOWN:** five differently named Dragons to hand, in full view — the single loudest signal this deck can send, and the moment three players start doing wrath math.
captions.Temur Ascendancy: **THE QUIET TELL:** three mana of haste-plus-draw that experienced tables read as a declaration of intent. Land it with the wave, not before it.

pilot_tips.text: Welcome the wrath you cannot stop — with Bidding in hand, their reset returns your whole graveyard of Dragons at once and re-fires every enters-trigger you own.

departments.pull_quote: You are never scarier than in the turns you are weakest — your whole political job is keeping the table's clock wrong about yours.

departments.headline: JAM, BAIT, OR WAIT?
departments.dek: One board asks whether nine mana of commander goes into five untapped Azorius lands; the other hands you a Tiamat trigger with a telegraphed board wipe across the table. Commit to your line out loud — then read ours.

callouts.title: SPREAD ONE — TURN 7
callouts.text: Urza's Incubator and Dragon's Hoard down, seven lands, The Ur-Dragon castable for seven with Heroic Intervention in hand — and the control player has five untapped lands and two counters already spent this game. Three branches: jam with backup, bait with Miirym, or hold everything.

callouts.title: SPREAD TWO — TURN 8
callouts.text: Tiamat just resolved and her search trigger is on the stack: up to five differently named Dragons, your pile to design — into seven lands of Supreme-Verdict-shaped mana. Which five names, and in what order do they hit the table? The pile IS the decision.

captions.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: **THE THREE-MANA QUESTION:** with Incubator and Eminence she costs {G}{U}{R} — the cheapest possible probe of a counter-heavy hand, and ward {2} taxes the answer either way.
captions.Heroic Intervention: **READ THE FINE PRINT:** hexproof and indestructible are shields for permanents you control. Your commander on the stack is a spell — this card has never once countered a Counterspell.

pilot_tips.text: Never hold Heroic Intervention as counterspell insurance — it protects permanents on the battlefield, and a commander on the stack is not yet one of them.

departments.pull_quote: Spend your one realistic cast when it is most likely to stick — and sequence the scariest piece last.
departments.note: Two spreads from decisions/001 and 002. The recommendation is revealed only after all branches, per the department's hard rule — and neither headline nor dek may telegraph it. Spread one's coaching carries the issue's best rules gotcha (protection cannot save a spell on the stack; a countered commander returns to the zone but the next cast is taxed); spread two's is a masterclass in wrath-math pile design, including the Courser rental that dodges the tax entirely. Branch citations (702.11b, 903.8, 903.9a) render with their ✓ treatment inside otherwise ★ spreads, exactly as the artifacts carry them.

departments.headline: WHO BEATS THE HOARD
departments.dek: One archetype owns your defining matchup, one simply out-clocks you, and two are softer than the table thinks. Know which seat at the pod is actually your problem — it is probably not the aggro deck.

threats.read: Your defining matchup: 24 threat bodies with the card advantage sitting on permanents means one wrath hits your board, your payoffs, and your draw layer at once. Commit exactly what wins before the wrath and no more, in waves. Your edge: the enchantment layer (Dragon Tempest, Temur Ascendancy, Garruk's Uprising) survives creature sweepers, and Patriarch's Bidding plus Haven of the Spirit Dragon rebuild cheaper than anything they can do — the wrath is often YOUR pivot point. Watch for exile and bounce wraths, which your indestructible package does not beat, and know that a quiet Rest in Peace deletes the whole rebuild plan.

Their inevitability beats your 8.989-turn clock, full stop. You hold exactly four relevant answers in 66 spells, so answer economy is everything: spend counters exclusively on spells that end the game, never on value pieces — the bar is 'ends the game', not 'looks scary'. Dovin's Veto is the one you save for the counter-war.

You are the control seat here: you cannot race (zero commander casts by turn 6), so you also do not try. Trade with big blockers, spend the sweepers on their board — Crux of Fate can destroy every non-Dragon and keep your entire hoard — and turn the corner the moment you stabilize. Their clock runs out of gas exactly when yours starts.

Taxes punish spell velocity, and you cast few, huge, double-discounted spells — Eminence plus Urza's Incubator plus Herald's Horn eat Thalia effects for breakfast, and your six spells-only lands keep working under most taxes because casting spells is all they ever did. An assembling lock still forces you into the beatdown role: race the lock's completion, not the pilot.

pilot_tips.text: Against creature decks, cast Crux of Fate on the mode that keeps your board — destroy all non-Dragons and attack into the wreckage.
Hold Dovin's Veto for the counter-war itself — it is the only answer you own that cannot be answered back.

departments.pull_quote: Four counterspells in sixty-six cards. Spend them on spells that end the game — never on the ones that merely look scary.

departments.headline: DISCOUNTS, DRAGONS, DETONATORS
departments.dek: Ninety-five entries doing five jobs: cheapen the Dragons, deploy the Dragons, pay off the Dragons, insure the Dragons, and — in exactly nine slots — answer everyone else. Rank matters, and the verified engines lead.

roster.role: The discount stack — the real commander
The draw layer — on permanents, on purpose
Interaction — all nine slots of it

captions.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: **SPELLS ONLY, AND WE MEAN ONLY:** this mana casts Dragon creature spells and nothing else — an activated ability is not a spell, so it cannot even pay Haven's own recursion mode. Six of your sources carry this restriction; count your unrestricted mana separately.
captions.Patriarch's Bidding: **THE REBUILD:** every Dragon in your graveyard returns at once, re-firing Tempest, Valkas, Terror, and Miirym on the way in. Mind the {B}{B} — black is the deck's thinnest colour, 11 land sources against a 36-source target.
captions.Mox Jasper: **DEAD ON ONE, FREE FOREVER AFTER:** zero mana, any colour — once you control a Dragon. Play it whenever it arrives; it costs nothing but patience.

pilot_tips.text: Pay Dragon's Hoard's draw activation with lands and rocks — none of the six spells-only sources can ever activate an ability, no matter how much Dragon mana is floating.

departments.note: Grouped by role, ranked by load: the two case-file engines open the page at feature scale, the discount stack second because it is the issue's thesis in card form. The interaction group's header does the teaching — nine answers is the linear-deck tradeoff, stated, not hidden. The bench strip is visually separated and labeled sideboard; its full 38-card story lives in Upgrade Watch. deck-facts caveat for the copy: 12 cards have no role-taxonomy entry, so role counts are floors, not exact numbers.

departments.headline: NINETY-EIGHT HANDS
departments.dek: Who painted your deck? Ninety-eight different people across forty-nine sets — no artist clears four cards, and the one we feature earned it by subject, not volume: he painted the commander this whole issue argues about.

featured.note: Let's be honest about the ranking first, because this department reads the table instead of quoting it: the count leaders are Adam Paquette, Grzegorz Rutkowski, and Kev Walker at four entries each, and the analysis itself says no standout — four cards is a cluster, not a signature, in a 133-entry pool where 98 artists appear. So the feature is an editorial choice, made openly: Jaime Jones painted three cards, and they happen to be the issue's spine — The Ur-Dragon himself, the commander on the cover; Temur Ascendancy, half of the pivot trigger this magazine keeps citing; and Dragonlord Kolaghan, the haste anthem that opens the window all by herself. Three cards, all in the 99, all load-bearing. Nobody curated this concentration — the analysis flags no collector-number runs and no roster overlap — it is simply where the pilot's printings landed, and that is the story: a deck assembled from forty-nine sets across two decades of the game, whose three most thesis-critical cards came from one hand anyway. Counting discipline, printed every issue: we count cards, never copies — Jonas De Ro's Mountain appears four times and Tomáš Honz's Forest three, and each is one entry; Mark Zug's tally includes Utvara Hellkite twice because the pilot owns a spare copy in the sideboard, and a spare is a printing fact, not a second painting.

also_worth_noting.note: Four entries, all in the 99, and the most strategically coherent cluster on the page: Urza's Incubator — the best card in the discount stack — Drakuseth, Maw of Flames, Sarkhan, Fireblood, and Rootbound Crag.
Four entries, three of them the mana: Blood Crypt, Cinder Glade, Steam Vents, plus Dragon's Hoard. The manabase-painter of the collection.
Four entries spanning main and bench: Dragonspeaker Shaman, Generous Gift, Witherbloom, the Balancer — and Rakdos Pit Dragon, which lives in the sideboard.
Three entries with an asterisk we print proudly: Faeburrow Elder, and Utvara Hellkite twice — the second a sideboard spare of the same card. Counted once where it counts.

captions.Dragonlord Kolaghan: **THE THIRD JONES:** a haste anthem on a 6/5 flier — the painting that opens the pivot window, from the same hand as the commander himself.
captions.The World Tree: **ART FILE FOOTNOTE:** Anastasia Ovchinnikova's lone credit is the land that turns the whole manabase any-colour at six lands — one card, one artist, maximum load.

departments.pull_quote: No artist owns this deck. Ninety-eight hands built the hoard — and we count the cards, not the copies.
departments.note: Renderer recomputes all counts from artist-credits: 133 entries, 138 copies, 98 artists, sideboard pool included in the totals and said so. Art File fast-facts: 49 sets, top sets Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander (17 entries) and Tarkir: Dragonstorm (13); treatments — 21 legendary frames, 11 enchantment frames, 2 borderless, 1 foil (the foil gets its sheen, a property of the physical card). No drop_runs reported, so no bought-whole caveat is needed beyond the sideboard-pool note.

departments.headline: MULLIGAN FOR FUNCTION
departments.dek: The sim keeps 76% of first sevens, so most hands are fine — the drill is spotting which of these four is the trap. Rule on each before you read the verdict, and remember: the commander is the one card you never mulligan toward.

hands.why: Three lands, ramp, an early payoff — and a cost reducer, the acceleration that matters most. The reducer-plus-ramp hand assembles by turn 6 in only 29.4% of games; when you are dealt one, you do not ship it hunting prettier Dragons.

Five lands and two haymakers is the classic trap seven: nothing to do until turn five, no reducer, no payoff, no protection. Lands plus seven-drops with no bridge is the named ship in this deck's mulligan rule.

Two lands rides on Sol Ring, and the rest is a deck in miniature: the deepest discount, the doubler, a payoff, and held protection — which the sim says you want in hand for the commit turn (66.4% of games have it by turn 6).

hands.verdict: SHIP — the colours can't cast it
hands.why: Three lands, zero blue or black sources — and this hand is blue-and-black shaped. Five colours is a real tax: black has just 11 land sources against Bidding's {B}{B}, and a hand whose colours cannot cast its spells is a mulligan no matter how good the spells are.

captions.Urza's Incubator: **THE KEEP SIGNAL:** a hand with a cost reducer is a keep almost regardless of what else it holds — the reducers, not the land drops, compress a nine-drop curve into a castable one.

pilot_tips.text: Count a protection spell as a keep-bonus, not a dead card — held cover is what authorizes the wave turn, and the free cast needs only your commander, who is guaranteed to show up eventually.

departments.pull_quote: You never mulligan for the commander — Eminence works from the command zone, so a hand that casts him is worth nothing extra.

departments.headline: BENCH PRESS
departments.dek: What do you do with a 38-card sideboard that is all Dragons? Judge every one. Two promotes, one bracket dial, three spares that were never legal options — and an obsolescence index that mostly concedes the deck already upgraded itself.

callouts.title: THE PROMOTES
callouts.text: Two swaps are unconditional. Deflecting Swat in for An Offer You Can't Refuse: it retargets the removal aimed at your commander or the counter aimed at Tiamat, it hits abilities — which nothing in the 99 does — and it never gifts the opponent two Treasures on the way out. Korlessa, Scale Singer in for Dragonlord's Servant: with 21 Dragon-typed cards plus Path of Ancestry and Herald's Horn rigging her top card, a two-mana engine that casts Dragons off the library beats the deck's seventh cost-reduction effect. Neither moves the bracket floor.

callouts.title: THE BRACKET DIAL
callouts.text: Aggravated Assault in for Crucible of Fire is a dial, not a default: the computed floor moves 3 → 4 the moment Assault enters the list, and that number changes which table the deck belongs at. The Savage Ventmaw loop it unlocks is checker-verified — unbounded combats, +1 mana per cycle, case file A-003 — and Crucible is the right cut because this deck wins on triggers, not on +3/+3. Bring it only to tables that agreed to it.

callouts.title: THE BENCH, JUDGED
callouts.text: Of the remaining 35: three are duplicate spares of maindeck cards (Old Gnawbone, Utvara Hellkite, Encroaching Dragonstorm) — a second copy is illegal in Commander, so they are spares, never options, and we say so instead of counting them. Sneak Attack stays benched by default: brilliant against counter-heavy pods, a waste of the Eminence discount everywhere else. Wrathful Red Dragon waits on a stack scenario — its Blasphemous Act interaction could turn your own sweeper into a table-kill, and it earns a slot the day the checker says so.

callouts.title: THE INDEX AUDIT
callouts.text: Run against this list, the obsolescence index mostly argues with itself: Klauth's listed successor is Savage Ventmaw — already in the deck. Skyshroud Claim's replacements are Farseek and Nature's Lore — in the deck beside it, because ramp redundancy is the strategy. And its Crux of Fate suggestions are worth ignoring out loud: no listed replacement can destroy every non-Dragon while sparing your board, and that one-sided mode is the entire slot. The machine cannot see typal constraints; we can.

captions.Aggravated Assault: **THE DIAL:** five mana of extra combats that Savage Ventmaw's attack trigger pays with one mana to spare — verified in case A-003, and the reason this card lives in the sideboard until the table votes on bracket 4.
captions.Korlessa, Scale Singer: **THE UNCONDITIONAL PROMOTE:** a two-mana engine that casts Dragons off the top of your library — in a deck with 21 Dragon-typed cards and two ways to rig the peek, she simply outworks a seventh discount.
captions.Sneak Attack: **THE SPECIALIST:** one red mana lands Drakuseth without casting it — countermagic never gets a window, and the end-step sacrifice even stocks Patriarch's Bidding. In pods without counter walls, it wastes the discount the deck is built on.

pilot_tips.text: Sleeve Deflecting Swat now, but read its free clause honestly — it costs nothing only while your commander is on the battlefield, so before the turn he lands you are paying retail for it, and it is still worth the slot.

departments.headline: THREE FILES, ONE ASTERISK
departments.dek: Every claim in this issue traces to one of three case files — 255 damage on a die roll, 64 on a cascade, and an unbounded combat loop that comes with a condition printed on the folder: the card is in the sideboard.
departments.note: Renderer-generated from the checker-passed artifacts; nothing summarized, truncated, or paraphrased — every citation verbatim in typewriter face against the June 19, 2026 rules. CASE A-002 (Miirym under Panharmonicon; pass — the full 12-step cascade with the 64-damage ledger and the finite-loop proof). The banner is a condition of publication, not a hedge — the loop's rules truth and the card's location are two separate facts and the file states both.

rhythm_notes: Canonical order alternates cleanly for this issue. The dense analysis of By the Numbers (five figure-heavy callouts) hands off to The Kill, which carries the issue's heaviest technical content but reads as narrative — the built-in breather doing its job — and The Kill is the peak, with A-001's numbered burst sequence as the volume's most ambitious spread. Politics Table (reflection) cools the reader before the participation spike of What's Your Play?; Know Your Enemy (reference, dense) is followed by the browsing-mode 99 and then Featured Artist, which serves as the issue's long exhale — deliberately unhurried after three consecutive strategy departments. Keep or Ship re-engages with practice mode before the low-intensity glide of Upgrade Watch (big this issue, but imagination-mode, not dense) into the opt-in depth of Judge's Desk. No two dense departments sit adjacent. Pun budget spent: EMINENCE DOMAIN and BENCH PRESS in headlines, plus 'we count it as a spare instead of pretending it's depth' as furniture wit — under the four-pun ceiling with room to spare.
